name: Surveys on developers' reliance on AI tools in 2026

source_tier: Company research and vendor surveys. None is peer-reviewed. Stack Overflow: platform-run community survey. Sonar, JetBrains and CoderPad: vendor surveys published as marketing or research-blog material. Devographics: independent community survey, reached here only through press.
access_status: Stack Overflow 2026: AI chapter, methodology page, landing page and announcement blog post opened live (read through a page-to-text fetch tool, so chart labels and prose were retrieved but full question wording is not shown on the page). Sonar 2026: full 57-page PDF downloaded and read directly as text, plus press release and blog. JetBrains: both research blog posts opened; the full 'State of Developer Ecosystem 2026' report page was not found (jetbrains.com/lp/devecosystem-2026/ returned 404 on 12 October 2026). CoderPad: report page opened. Devographics: primary site NOT opened, press coverage only.
author_credentials: Stack Overflow (Stack Exchange Inc.): Q&A platform whose traffic has fallen with AI use and which sells data licensing and AI products; it has an interest in findings about trust and source attribution. Sonar: sells code quality and verification software (SonarQube); the 'verification gap' framing supports its product, as The Register noted on 9 January 2026. JetBrains: sells IDEs and its own AI assistant and agent (Junie); author Mikhail Bogdanov writes for JetBrains Research. CoderPad: sells technical hiring assessments; its report argues AI is 'essential infrastructure' and that assessments should allow AI. Devographics: independent survey group behind State of JS and State of CSS.
exact_quotes: Stack Overflow 2026 AI chapter, section heading: '31% of daily AI users use it for 4+ hours/day'
Stack Overflow 2026 AI chapter: 'Of the over 70% of respondents who use AI daily, 31% use it over four hours per day.'
Stack Overflow 2026 AI chapter: 'AI has become less sidekick and more infrastructure, built right into the tools technologists already use.'

Stack Overflow 2026 AI chapter: 'When asked when it's acceptable to trust AI, 48% indicate they trust AI when they can easily validate the answers' and 'only 16% extend that trust to most tasks that are not important work decisions.'
Stack Overflow 2026 AI chapter, section heading: '6 out of 10 users cite a reason to avoid using AI at work or school, losing job skills is a top concern.'

Stack Overflow 2026 AI chapter, chart response option: 'Concern over losing job skills or training an AI to replace you' (2,367 responses, 17.1%); 'I do not avoid using AI at work or school' (5,728, 41.3%).

Stack Overflow 2026 methodology: '30,903 responses from 169 countries are used in these survey results.' Data 'recorded from June 23, 2026 through August 5, 2026.' 'The survey was promoted through stackoverflow.com, stackoverflow.blog and our email list.'

Stack Overflow blog, 6 October 2026: '73% of respondents who indicate using AI coding assistants/agents use them daily'; '62% of all respondents view AI at least somewhat positively, while that jumps to 71% for daily users'; 'a large majority (79%) want to upskill their AI game'.

Sonar 2026 report, p.4 'About this report': 'The 2026 State of Code Developer Survey was a quantitative online survey conducted among professional software developers. Fieldwork for the survey ran throughout October 2025. The final sample size for the study included 1,149 responses, distributed globally.' Respondents had to 'have used AI as part of their job within the past year.'

Sonar 2026 report, p.5: '72% of developers who have tried AI coding tools now use them every day.' Question: 'How frequently (do you / your team or company) use AI coding tools in your development workflow?' Multiple times a day 42%, Daily 30%, A few times a week 15%, Weekly 7%, Occasionally 6% (n=1,148).

Sonar 2026 report, p.9: '96% of developers don't fully trust that AI-generated code is functionally correct.' Item: 'I trust that AI code is functionally correct': Completely agree 4%, Somewhat agree 25%, Somewhat disagree 31%, Completely disagree 17%.

Sonar 2026 report, p.29, 'Top 10 concerns', share 'Extremely / Very Concerned': 'Over-reliance on AI leading to a decline in the team's understanding of the codebase 53%'; 'Deskilling or erosion of our own coding abilities 48%' (n=1,149).

Sonar 2026 report, p.42: 'Senior developers also express less anxiety about the long-term impact of AI on their skills, with 41% concerned about the erosion of their personal coding abilities (vs. 50% of junior developers) and 45% worried about a decline in codebase understanding (vs. 56% of junior developers).'

Sonar 2026 report, p.39: '62% say they have more time to advance their skills, far outpacing the 51% of' senior developers (item: 'I have more time to spend on advancing my skills than before I used AI').

JetBrains, August 2026: '90% of professional developers were using AI coding agents at work at least weekly' with '68% using them daily' (May to July 2026; 'more than 15,000 professional developers worldwide').
JetBrains, April 2026: '90% of developers regularly used at least one AI tool at work for coding and development tasks' (AI Pulse, January 2026, 'over 10,000 professional developers worldwide').

CoderPad 2026, question: 'If AI tools were removed tomorrow, your productivity would...' Drop by more than 25%: 10%; Drop by 10-25%: 44%; No change: 34%; Improve: 5%; Not sure: 7%. Summary line: '54% of developers would lose some of their productivity if AI tools were removed tomorrow.'
key_claims: Stack Overflow 2026: AI use among respondents is close to universal and heavy. Among those answering the hours question, about 80% use AI an hour or more a day and under 1% report none. Stack Overflow describes AI as 'less sidekick and more infrastructure'.
Stack Overflow 2026: trust is conditional. The largest group (48%) trusts AI when answers are easy to validate; 16% extend trust to most tasks that are not important work decisions.
Stack Overflow 2026: about six in ten respondents give a reason to avoid AI at work or school, and the most common reason is concern over losing job skills or training an AI to replace them (17.1%).

Sonar 2026: 72% of developers who have used AI use it daily, 96% do not fully trust AI code to be functionally correct, and 48% always check AI-assisted code before committing. Sonar calls this a 'verification gap'.

Sonar 2026: 48% are extremely or very concerned about 'deskilling or erosion of our own coding abilities' and 53% about over-reliance eroding the team's understanding of the codebase. Junior developers are more worried than senior ones (50% vs 41%).

JetBrains 2026: 90% of professional developers use AI coding agents at work at least weekly and 68% daily (May to July 2026). The same 90% headline figure for 'at least one AI tool' already held in January 2026.
CoderPad 2026: 54% of developers say their productivity would drop by 10% or more if AI tools were removed tomorrow; 34% say no change; 5% say it would improve. CoderPad reads this as dependency.

On the direct question: no survey opened here asks developers whether they would be willing to work without AI, or whether they would refuse to. The closest items are CoderPad's hypothetical about productivity if AI were removed, Sonar's concern item about deskilling, and Stack Overflow's reasons-for-avoiding-AI item. None measures willingness.
headline_figures: Stack Overflow 2026, hours of AI use per day (n=10,926): 4+ hours 30.9%; 2-4 hours 24.1%; 1-2 hours 25.3%; under 1 hour every day 12.2%; under 1 hour and not every day 7.0%; none 0.5%. Fieldwork 23 June to 5 August 2026.
Stack Overflow 2026: 73% of respondents who use AI coding assistants or agents use them daily (blog, 6 October 2026). Base is users of those tools, not all respondents.
Stack Overflow 2026: 48% trust AI when they can easily validate the answers; 16% trust it for most tasks that are not important work decisions. No n shown on the page.

Stack Overflow 2026, reasons for avoiding AI at work or school (n=13,857): do not avoid 41.3%; concern over losing job skills or training an AI to replace you 17.1%; moral or ethical concerns 15.2%; privacy or security 13.0%; environmental 8.2%; other 2.7%; difficulty or lack of training 2.6%.
Stack Overflow 2026: 62% of all respondents view AI at least somewhat positively, 71% among daily users (blog).
Sonar 2026 (n=1,148, October 2025 fieldwork): 42% use AI coding tools multiple times a day and 30% daily, giving the 72% 'every day' figure. Base is developers who used AI at work in the past year.

Sonar 2026: 96% do not fully trust that AI-generated code is functionally correct (i.e. 4% 'completely agree' that they trust it; 25% somewhat agree). 48% always check AI-assisted code before committing.
Sonar 2026: 42% of committed code reported as AI-generated or assisted, expected to reach 65% by 2027, up from 6% in 2023 (self-reported estimates).

Sonar 2026 (n=1,149): 48% extremely or very concerned about deskilling or erosion of own coding abilities; 53% about over-reliance leading to a decline in the team's understanding of the codebase. By experience: deskilling 50% (10 years or fewer) vs 41% (20 years or more).
JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026 (more than 15,000 professional developers, May to July 2026): 90% use AI coding agents at work at least weekly; 68% daily.
JetBrains AI Pulse, January 2026 (over 10,000 professional developers): 90% regularly used at least one AI tool at work for coding; 74% had adopted specialised AI developer tools.

CoderPad State of Tech Hiring 2026 (about 650 participants, developers and recruiters combined): productivity if AI tools removed tomorrow: drop over 25% 10%; drop 10-25% 44%; no change 34%; improve 5%; not sure 7%.

Devographics State of Web Dev AI 2026 (7,258 developers, per The Register, 21 May 2026): 74% agreed AI tools are integral to their workflow; 63% use AI to generate more than half their code. [uncertain: primary not opened]
sample_and_method: All are self-report surveys; none is randomised or observational. Stack Overflow 2026: 30,903 responses from 169 countries, 23 June to 5 August 2026, opt-in, recruited through stackoverflow.com, its blog and email list; per-question bases are much smaller (about 11,000 to 14,000 on the AI items). Sonar 2026: online quantitative survey, 1,149 professional developers, fieldwork October 2025, screened to people who had used AI at work in the past year; recruitment method and panel provider not stated in the report. JetBrains Developer Ecosystem 2026: more than 15,000 professional developers, figures for May to July 2026, regional quotas, reweighted by region, employment status, language and familiarity with JetBrains products. JetBrains AI Pulse January 2026: over 10,000 professional developers, recruited mainly through debranded Instagram ads (Zhihu in China) with about 16% from the JetBrains panel; raking weights. CoderPad 2026: about 650 participants across developers and recruiters; 47% of developer respondents had 0 to 3 years' experience; sampling method, dates and weighting not stated.
evidence_offered: Self-reported frequencies, attitudes and estimates. No survey observes behaviour. The CoderPad productivity figures and Sonar's '42% of committed code' are respondents' own estimates. No survey links answers to task records, commits or any measured output.
data_vintage: Stack Overflow 2026: fieldwork 23 June to 5 August 2026, results published 6 October 2026 (six days before this research was done; full data set promised but not yet seen). Sonar '2026' report: fieldwork October 2025, published 8 January 2026, so its data predate METR's February 2026 update. JetBrains: January 2026 (AI Pulse) and May to July 2026 (Developer Ecosystem), published April and August 2026. CoderPad: published 11 February 2026, fieldwork dates not stated.
figure_provenance: Stack Overflow 30.9% using AI 4+ hours a day: from the AI chapter chart (3,378 of 10,926). The page prose words it as '31% of daily AI users', and the blog says 'a third of daily users'. The chart percentage is of all who answered the question, so the 'of daily users' wording and the 30.9% do not quite match (of daily users only it would be about 33%).
Stack Overflow 'over 70% use AI daily' (AI chapter prose) vs '73% of those using coding assistants or agents use them daily' (blog): different bases. Neither is a share of all 30,903 respondents.

Stack Overflow trust: the AI chapter gives 48% and 16%. Trade press (IT Brief) reports 'only 6.6% would trust it for important decisions' and '78.7% said attribution was important or very important'; the blog says source attribution is required for trust by 93%. The 6.6%, 78.7% and 93% figures were not located on the AI chapter page. A fetch summary of the landing page also returned 'over 87% have some level of trust, up from 31% last year'; that sentence was not found on the AI chapter and must not be cited without checking. [uncertain]

Stack Overflow 17.1% 'losing job skills': the response option is double-barrelled ('losing job skills or training an AI to replace you'), and the shares sum to 100%, which suggests a single-choice item or shares of total selections rather than a multi-select prevalence.
Sonar 72%, 96%, 48%, 53%: all read directly from the report PDF (pp. 5, 9, 29, 42) and match the press release and blog.

Sonar 96%: derived as everyone except the 4% who 'completely agree' that they trust AI code is functionally correct. 29% agree at least somewhat, so '96% do not trust' overstates it; the report's own wording is 'don't fully trust'.
JetBrains 90% and 68%: from the August 2026 research blog. i-programmer gives different fieldwork dates (April to May 2026); JetBrains' own post says May to July 2026.

CoderPad 54%: sum of 'drop by more than 25%' (10%) and 'drop by 10-25%' (44%). The report words it two ways, 'lose some of their productivity' and 'drops of 10% or more'; the second is accurate to the options.

A Feedbagel headline ('Study finds most developers refuse to code without AI') attributes a 'most developers refuse' claim to METR's February 2026 study. No survey supports 'most refuse'; this is press paraphrase of METR and was not checked here.
population_and_transfer: Stack Overflow: self-selected visitors and mailing-list members, global, skewed to engaged users of a site whose audience has changed since 2023. Sonar: only developers who already used AI at work in the past year, so non-users are excluded by design. JetBrains: professional developers, quota-sampled and weighted, the nearest to a general population estimate but recruited by ads. CoderPad: small, and nearly half the developer respondents are early-career. Usage-frequency findings transfer reasonably to engineers in ordinary companies; attitude percentages should be treated as indicative, not as population estimates.
outcome_measured: None of the listed outcomes directly. These surveys measure self-reported usage frequency, trust, sentiment, concern about skills, and (CoderPad only) a hypothetical self-estimate of productivity without AI. No employment, task speed, retention or on-the-job performance is measured.
limitations_stated: Stack Overflow's 2026 methodology page describes validity and bot-flagging rules but states no sampling limitations (as retrieved). Sonar states only: 'Percentages in this report may not sum to exactly 100% due to rounding or multi-select questions. All data is based on the total sample of 1,149 respondents unless otherwise noted.' and that respondents had 'used AI as part of their job within the past year'. JetBrains' posts have no limitations section; they note the promo avoided mentioning AI so as not to attract enthusiasts or sceptics. CoderPad states none. Devographics, as reported by The Register, said the topic may have 'biased the respondent set towards developers who do have an interest in AI'.
counter_evidence: Within the same surveys: CoderPad's own data has 34% saying no change and 5% saying productivity would improve without AI, so 39% do not report dependence, and 44% of the 54% expect only a 10-25% drop. Stack Overflow reports about six in ten giving a reason to avoid AI, and 20% keep it away from production operations. Sonar finds 96% do not fully trust AI code. Heavy use sits alongside limited trust, which cuts against reading usage as contented dependence. Self-estimated productivity is also weak evidence: METR's 2025 trial found developers estimated a speed-up when measured results showed a slowdown.
alternative_explanations: High daily use can reflect employer mandates, tool defaults (AI built into IDEs and search) and rational preference, not inability to work without it. Stack Overflow's 'infrastructure' framing supports the built-in reading. Opt-in samples over-represent engaged, tool-using developers; Sonar screens out non-users altogether. Concern about deskilling (Sonar 48%) is a worry about the future, not a report that skills have declined. CoderPad's sample is nearly half early-career developers, who report the largest gains in Sonar's data, so its 54% may overstate the general figure. Vendor framing: each publisher benefits from its headline.
verification_status: VERIFIED at primary (opened): Stack Overflow 2026 hours-per-day distribution, 48% and 16% trust figures, avoidance chart including 17.1% job-skills item, 30,903 responses, 169 countries, fieldwork dates, 6 October 2026 publication, 73% daily (of assistant/agent users), 62% and 71% sentiment. Read via a fetch tool that summarises the page, so wording of short quotes should be re-checked by eye before publishing.

VERIFIED at primary (PDF text read directly): every Sonar figure listed, with page numbers, including fieldwork October 2025, n=1,149, 72%, 96%, 48% deskilling, 53% over-reliance, 50% vs 41% by experience, 62% vs 51% time for skills.
VERIFIED at primary (opened): JetBrains 90% weekly, 68% daily, more than 15,000, May to July 2026; AI Pulse 90%, 74%, over 10,000, January 2026.
VERIFIED at primary (opened): CoderPad question wording and all five response shares, about 650 participants, published 11 February 2026.

NOT VERIFIED: Stack Overflow 6.6%, 78.7% (trade press only), '87% some trust, up from 31%' (fetch summary of landing page, not confirmed on the AI chapter); exact Stack Overflow question wording (not shown on results pages); Devographics figures (press only); JetBrains full 2026 report (not found).

NEGATIVE FINDING, stated plainly: none of the surveys opened (Stack Overflow 2026, Sonar 2026, JetBrains 2026 posts, CoderPad 2026) asks developers whether they would be willing to work without AI. This rests on the published results pages and the full Sonar report; the Stack Overflow and JetBrains questionnaires themselves were not available to check, so an unpublished item cannot be ruled out.
relevance_to_essay: Supports the background claim that AI use is now the default: 68% to 73% daily use, under 1% of Stack Overflow's AI-question respondents reporting none. That makes a no-AI arm unrepresentative of normal work and harder to recruit for. It does not show that developers refuse to work without AI. No survey asks that, so METR's 30% to 50% remains the only figure on tasks actually withheld, and the thought should say so.
implications_for_measurement: Surveys can tell leaders how much AI is used and how it is trusted, not what it does to output. Three usable points. First, with daily use this common, a clean without-AI comparison inside one team is closer to a deprivation test than a baseline, so before-and-after or between-team comparisons on delivery records are more realistic than a control group. Second, self-estimates (CoderPad's 54%, Sonar's 35% average productivity boost) should not stand in for measurement. Third, the surveys point at what is worth measuring instead: verification effort (Sonar: 38% say reviewing AI code takes more effort, 48% always check) and codebase understanding (53% worried), which delivery speed alone will miss.
open_questions: Whether any 2026 survey asks directly about willingness to work without AI (none found). Exact question wording and bases for Stack Overflow's trust and avoidance items, pending the public data set. Whether the JetBrains full 2026 report includes skills or dependence items. Whether Sonar's deskilling concern corresponds to any measured decline. How CoderPad recruited and when it fielded.
